articles.title: Skirts given star billing as Prada swerves trousers and dresses in Milan
articles.summary: Combination of Miuccia Prada with Belgian designer Raf Simons once again spins gold for fashion house. Miuccia Prada’s style formula is simple: begin with a great skirt. Her personal uniform is a knee-length skirt, A-line or pleated, most often with a plain sweater and kitten heels.
body: The Prada collection that opened Milan fashion week made a compelling case for her favourite outfit, with a skirt the star of every one of the 63 looks – no dresses, no trousers. It won the room over, so expect to see the personality skirt on a high street near you soon.

For the past six years, Miuccia Prada has shared design duties with Belgian designer Raf Simons, 20 years her junior. The arrangement was considered unusual when announced, but the house of Prada has always had a way of spinning gold from quirky ideas, and it has worked.
“She had the idea to focus on skirts this time,” Simons explained before this show. “And I said, why not make it an all-skirt show?”

She prefers skirts to dresses because “they give you room for contrast”, Mrs Prada said. “The way I think and feel is complicated, contradictory. If I wear something feminine, I want to wear something masculine too. A dress is all one idea, and we are never just one idea.”
points: Combination of Miuccia Prada with Belgian designer Raf Simons once again spins gold for fashion house.

articles.title: Why you should quit and not look back: ‘Saying yes to everything is saying no to what matters’
articles.summary: In her new book, The Case For Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out, Lindsay Crouse discusses the costs and traps of never giving up – and how she set herself free. Lindsay Crouse used to define herself as not a quitter.
body: She went to Harvard University, where she learned to become even more high-achieving and ambitious, then landed an assistant job at the New York Times and worked her way up to become an opinion writer and producer. On the weekends, Crouse ran marathons and did endurance sports, clocking new personal bests throughout her thirties.
“My entire life was really guided by only one question: how can I go harder, and do more?” she says now over Zoom.

Over time, though, that mentality began to backfire. After having two children, Crouse started falling behind, dropping balls and losing her passion for running and writing. Something needed to change.

Now Crouse argues quitting is essential for a satisfying, successful life. She herself left her prestigious job to chase unknown risks and rewards. “We need to start viewing quitting as a tool of perseverance, rather than the enemy of it,” she said. “If we find ourselves in a hole, often we dig harder when we should just stop digging.”

articles.title: Chanel and Tribeca Called in Some Hollywood Help to Kick Off the Through Her Lens Program
articles.summary: Tuesday afternoon’s luncheon marked the beginning of the annual three-day workshop, now in its 11th edition. Among those who joined Rosenthal were this year’s jury members Halle Berry, Regina King, and Autumn Durald Arkapaw, as well as mentor Celine Song, who debuted her baby bump on the red carpet…
body: According to Jane Rosenthal, three words can change an aspiring filmmaker’s life. She wasn’t referring to Through Her Lens —although Tribeca and Chanel’s long-running program for women and non-binary auteurs can and does do just that. Rather, she was reminding a room full of powerful people—actors, directors, and executives—to just “read the script” when they are given an opportunity to do so.

The CEO of Tribeca, who started her career in 1975 as one of very few women in the room, recalled a formative moment when she fought hard to bring a project about domestic violence to the screen, despite numerous objections. The movie in question, based on a true story, ended up being The Burning Bed, with Farrah Fawcett playing the lead. Not only did it win awards; it prompted national conversation around the pervasive issue once it saw the light of day. “That moment taught me something very early on: It matters who is in the room. It matters even more who has the power, and who is willing to say, “Yes. Read the script. Listen to her.”

articles.title: Ejae Walks Vogue World: Milan 2026 in Archival Roberto Capucci Fit for a Royal
articles.summary: Walking in an opulent blue and black tiered gown, singer and style star Ejae was a part of the show’s opening chapter, Act I: The Artisanal Revolution.
body: This evening, at Vogue World: Milano, singer and style star Ejae walked the runway in an archival Roberto Capucci gown. The blue-and-black tiered gown is a prime example of the Italian master’s craftsmanship.

Born in Rome in 1930, Capucci originally trained as a sculptor before opening his first clothing atelier, all before the age of 20. In the aftermath of World War II, Capucci, alongside Valentino Garavani and Emilio Pucci, became the leading fashion designers of their time, ushering in an opulent era of Italian design. A passionate and colorful artisan, Capucci’s work can be recognized through his exuberant color play and often sculptural silhouettes. As reported by Joan Juliet Buck in Vogue in 1989, Italian model Mirella Petteni even stored her two Capucci dresses each in their own closet in her Venetian home.

articles.title: Inside ‘Sterling Point’ Star Bo Bragason’s First Fashion Week
articles.summary: Ahead of the Prada spring 2027 show, ‘Sterling Point’ star Bo Bragason brings Vogue along to her first Milan Fashion Week. On the agenda? Black coffee and power suits.
body: Bo Bragason is feeling “blessed.” Yes, her flight out to Milan was delayed and yes, she only has 48 hours in the city before she has to get back to work (“I’m a busy girl”), but none of that is dampening her mood. The actor is about to attend her first fashion week—kicking off her front row career with the Prada spring 2027 show, no less. “It’s so insane,” she says, laughing. “I really can’t believe it.”

Bragason—who stole hearts as the carefree Oona in the hit teen drama Sterling Point this summer—is particularly excited about being a Prada attendee. So much so that she confesses she couldn’t sleep last night. “Prada? Yeah, it’s sick,” she calls to tell me from her hotel the day before. “It’s literally the best introduction [to fashion].” For the occasion, a relaxed charcoal grey suit worn over a crisp shirt in powder blue. “It’s a power suit type of moment,” Bragason confirms. “It’s very androgynous, which I love.”

articles.title: The Best Boxed Stuffing Mix, According to Our Taste Test
articles.summary: We tasted seven popular stuffing mixes from Stove Top, Pepperidge Farm, Trader Joe’s, and more. These three came out on top.
body: Boxed stuffing may not taste exactly like homemade stuffing, but when Thanksgiving prep starts to feel chaotic, a good mix is a shortcut worth taking.

The best boxed stuffing should have the hallmarks of a great homemade version: a soft, fluffy interior, a crisp, bronzed top, and plenty of buttery, savory flavor. We looked for mixes with distinct pieces of bread that absorbed moisture without turning soggy or stodgy, plus enough sage, rosemary, parsley, and other aromatics to make every bite taste like Thanksgiving.

We tested seven popular boxed stuffing mixes to find the ones worth serving. Stove Top Savory Herbs was our favorite overall, Stove Top Traditional Sage was the herbiest, and Pepperidge Farm Herb-Seasoned Classic Stuffing had the freshest flavor and texture.

The clear favorite in our taste test, Stove Top Savory Herbs has an ingredient list similar to our runner up, Stove Top Traditional Sage with one noteworthy difference. Savory Herbs includes MSG, which gives this mix its extra savory boost.

articles.title: Maybe Don't Bring Your Iced Coffee to a Job Interview
articles.summary: Experts weigh in on the etiquette question that's been lighting up the internet.
body: In an era when everyone totes water bottles from the gym, to breakfast meetings, to the office, and then to dinner, the lines of personal beverage etiquette have blurred.
This week’s topic of debate: Is it ok to bring an iced coffee to a job interview?

The discourse wildfire was first sparked by a TikTok post from Caitlin Wehniainen, a recruiter “with 16 years of experience” who “deals with mostly Fortune 500, super buttoned up operations,” as she describes it. She argues that the Gen Z candidates she sees arriving at job interviews with iced coffee in hand appear unprofessional.

“When you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte,” Wehniainen says in the video, it makes it look like “this interview is just like a stop on your list of errands for the day.” It looks too casual, and it makes a bad impression.
